Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant interest from researchers for its potential to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems. Nevertheless, existing single- or dual-target CDR techniques frequently face limitations, including the requirement that at least one domain contains sufficient data and their strong reliance on domain-invariant preferences. These assumptions are often unrealistic in scenarios where domains are sparse, as both source and destination fields may lack adequate information. Instead of assuming that preferences remain consistent, this paper presents MultSDCR—a multisparse-domain collaborative recommendation model based on aspect-based learning designed for environments where multiple sparse domains exist. Our approach aims to enhance preference accuracy by assuming users maintain stability in certain preferences across domains while others vary. Specifically, MultSDCR separates preferences into aspect-level components to foster cross-domain collaborative learning. Additionally, it incorporates a novel mechanism for multissargeted transfer learning characterized by adaptive and domain-specific modulation. Experiments conducted on diverse real-world sparse datasets confirm that MultSDCR significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Rapid increases in MRI datasets, particularly those at large scales, make automated quality control (QC) critical. Our focus centered on MRIQC preprocessing, testing the pipeline both with and without these steps; we additionally examined the distribution of site- and study-level classification probabilities for models trained without preprocessing using ABIDE and CATI data. Simulation outcomes are rigorously contrasted with the standard well-mixed model to reveal notable discrepancies in both the spatial concentration profiles and the volume of inhaled viral particles. Most specifically, at low mechanical air velocities, well-predetermined well mixing models predict that viral loads will be over-predicted near the infected individual and over-predicted near others. The findings reported herein are universally significant for other enclosed areas.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves the enhancement of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in materials positioned near an interface with a high-SOC constituent; this phenomenon is observable in systems like ferromagnetic layers and graphene. Regulating SOC serves as a potential avenue for uncovering exotic novel states, particularly within superconductors and semimetals. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport of Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, aiming to identify signatures of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and determine its origin. Our findings suggest a pronounced increase in Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy for both longitudinal resistivity and anomalous hall resistivity as the Cobalt layer becomes very thin. Furthermore, analyzing the skew-scattering component of the anomalous Hall resistivity indicates that Bi-inducing alterations shifts scattering to an extrinsic skew-scattering regime. These results suggest the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect likely stems from the elastic interaction of Cobalt free carriers with Bismuth sites located at the interface.

This study explores imposing explicit Lipschitz constraints on neural network architectures to ensure stability with respect to inputs. We introduce a method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for typical feedforward layers and use it to frame neural network training with bounded dynamics as a constrained optimization task soluble via projected stochastic gradients. Results reveal these models outperform those trained using standard regularizers. Furthermore, we show that the hyperparameters require only intuitive adjustment and illustrate how selecting a specific norm influences the model. Lastly, our approach yields distinct performance advantages even when only limited data is available for training.

To address recent indications of lepton-flavour non-universality observed in $b \to c \ell \nu$ and $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions, this investigation examines Drell-Yan dipositron pairs at CERN's LHC. Framework theories featuring vector leptoquarks that couple to third-generation fermions serve as the basis for computing full ${\cal O} (\alpha_s)$ corrections to the production rate, enabling the generation of parton showers at Next-to-Leading Order plus next-to-leading log (NLO $+$PS) precision via POWHEG. The work includes the development of specialized Monte Carlo software that dynamically computes NLO QCD corrections by interfacing with PYTHIA. Using this implementation, we simulate invariant-mass distributions for $τ^+ τ^+$ and $μ^+ τ^+$ combinations at CMS with NLO QCD accuracy. These high-precision $tt^*$ (NLO$+$PS) simulations provide the foundation for robust experiments capable of identifying resonances at the 1.3 and $1.6$ TeV level. Such potential discoveries would validate existing non-universality models as they stand, although the result would necessitate separate leptoquark states in both the charm-seasector to preserve unitarity.

Radiation constraints inherent to positron emission tomography (PET) imaging hinder its application for studying vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children, adults needing frequent scans. Decreasing radiotracer doses or scan duration reduces the count of photons, thereby compromising image quality. While recent algorithms based on deep neural networks (DNN) utilizing image-to-image translation can transform pairings of high-contrast MRI and low-dose—yet low-resolution—PET scans into high-quality PET images, these current models often assume test data closely mirrors training data statistically and lack robust evaluation metrics for novel, out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. This paper proposes a new DNN approach that (i) incorporates the fundamental sinogram physics of PET systems and (ii) quantifies the uncertainty predicted by the network via the heteroscedastic residuals between predicted and reference signals across each voxel. Named suDNN, this uncertainty-aware, physics-informed framework reconstructs standard-dose PET images by integrating low-dose PET input with corresponding multi-sequence MRI data, significantly enhancing DNN performance on OOD datasets. Empirical results drawn from both synthetic and genuine experiments validate that suDNN outperforms current baselines in accuracy, consistency, and durability when handling OOD cases.

Centering Theory (Grosz et al., 1995) analyzes how the structural components of conversation maintain local coherence through successive utterances referencing shared entities. This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and current coreference resolution systems. We systematically assess whether neural coreference solvers align with Centering Theory rules by operationalizing the theory, constructing discourse-specific metrics, and employing a search-based framework. Results from an information-theoretic approach indicate a positive correlation between centering concepts and coreference; however, they suggest high-performing neural resolvers derive limited additional advantage from explicitly integrating these ideas. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that pretrained context-aware embeddings inherently encode much of this coherence information, which likely explains why Centering Theory yields minimal improvements for models using such representations. Lastly, we discuss known coreference drivers unmodeled by the original CT, such as world knowledge and temporal preferences. We propose an adapted version of CT incorporating recency bias, demonstrating that it more accurately captures coreference patterns than the unmodified theory.

WiFi fingerprints, which utilize collected Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) references for known locations, have emerged as the primary indoor positioning method, but effectively estimating the spatial relationship between these fingerprints is heavily influenced by the choice of signal distance function. This study introduces a machine learning approach to estimate signal distance based on actual physical or geometric distance. To facilitate this estimation, we developed a novel, robust, and computationally efficient directed graph-based distance metric. Furthermore, we evaluate multiple machine learning regression models to identify the optimal algorithm for utilizing this new metric for indoor positioning.

We propose leveraging machine-learning (ML) image processing innovations to analyze all-sky maps (ASM) collected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. A one-year ASM was synthetically extended from an eight-week legacy one-week image simulation through three automated techniques: "dictionary learning," "noise suppression," and "image translation." Despite noisier model estimates than traditional likelihood analysis, these algorithms produced noticeable smoothing without constraints from prior astrophysical models. Of particular note were complex galactic plane emissions mirrored from seven-day data against simulated ground truth from an eight-week timescale simulation. Deviations between our synthesized ML results and standard ground truth maps are largely due to long-term variability in AGN fluxes over an eight-week timescale; these models could even isolate AGN activity objectively and automatedly. Through this approach, fainter, extended, and previously unseen features across multiple frequency regimes are revealed with enhanced clarity.

Inspired by the effectiveness of serial dictatorship in social choice scenarios, we investigate its potential in solving diverse combinatorial optimization challenges. We propose an abstract model where a sequence of agent movements—an order termed the "action sequence"—dictates individual roles. Each agent optimizes her outcome given the choices made by preceding participants, with our aim to identify sequences that maximize total agent utility, known as social welfare. We assume the ability to query value functions based on an agent acting after any specific preceding subset $S$. In this abstract setting, we derive state-of-the-art polynomial queries for social welfare maximization. Specifically, we design query algorithms leveraging the structure where an agent's value depends on the sequence formed by subsequent participants. We establish general welfare theoretical upper bounds dependent on the width $w$, defined as the maximum, across all contexts, of the minimal sequence segment required for an agent to exhibit non-constant utility; this metric applies, for instance, in combinatorial auction environments. Using these bounds as guidance, we identify efficient polynomial querying algorithms. We also confirm tightness of these bounds in combinatorial auctions involving uniform agent values and other classic optimization problems found within computer science. Collectively, our work offers an optimistic viewpoint: combinatoriated puzzle-like efforts to global optimization can be triggered by localized, decentralized actions.

We have created two unique techniques to analyze point spread functions (PSFs) for detecting binary asteroid systems using extensive archival data from the Pan-STARRS1 3g Drift Scan. Using simulated data, we validated the effectiveness of the proposed methods, allowing us to examine real images of asteroid 2665 Demidenchov and successfully identify a binary system with a 10-arcsecond orbital period.

This paper introduces several variations of Leibniz rules specifically formulated for Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators. It establishes the fundamental rules of multiplication, division, and chaining—known respectively as the product, quotient, and chain rules—applied to both types of operators. A distinct feature of this work involves four distinct categories of product rules: Product Rule I, Product Rule II, Product Rule III, and Product Rule IV. Similarly, the quotient rule is developed into four corresponding types based on these product variants. Additionally, the paper defines four separate classifications for the chain rule: Chain Rule I, Chain Rule II, and two others up to Type IV.

We introduce G4C (Goal-driven Guidance Generation in Grounded Communication), a new framework dedicated to investigating natural language interactions driven by specific objectives. We select Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our testing environment; this role-playing ecosystem brings together various player characters and a Dungeon Master, whose collective aim is to achieve player-benefiting objectives. In this setup, student personas act as players defining unique attributes, while the Dungeon Master, functioning as both the rule-enforcing judge and guide, steers these students toward an ultimate shared goal. We outline a theory-of-mind-based approach for employing reinforcement learning to characterize this Dungeon Master, involving two key steps: (1) forecasting student reactions to specific utterances using archived D&D transcripts, and (2) constructing a utility function that reflects the effectiveness of guidance based on those predicted responses. To validate our framework and algorithm, we perform extensive simulations within the open-ended GPT-based "Midnight GP" digital D&D platform. Our results include a detailed examination of the learnedD&D guidance strategy.

Remote epitaxy using monolayer graphene is advantageous for generating materials with significant lattice mismatches, peeling off standalone membranes, and recycling cost-intensive wafers. Nevertheless, direct empirical proof of this distant growth mode has historically been missing because impurities at the graphene-substrate junction often allow competing theories—such as lateral growth initiated through defects or Van der Waals alignment—to account for the resulting single-crystalline layers. In this study, depositing the Heusler alloy GdPtSb onto purified graphene atop sapphire yielded a distinct epitaxial superstructure rotated by 30° that is ruled out by both pinhole-based or Van der Waals mechanisms. As growth temperatures drop, this 30° domain grows in proportion to the direct (0°) alignment; we attribute this shift to reduced surface mobility at lower heat, which promotes remote growth, whereas high heat facilitates faster surface diffusion that supports pinhole-driven epitaxis. Furthermore, achieving substrate-oriented epitaxy for diverse Heuslers like LaPtSb and GdAuGe requires thermal cycling the graphene/substrate assembly to ~700\^CC alongside precise accounting of lattice mismatch errors between both film interfaces. The observation of this 30° superstructure serves as an experimental signature for remote epitaxis, uniquely ruling out the primary alternative mechanisms discussed earlier.

The provenances of high-energy gamma-rays originating from prominent local radio galaxies remain unclear. We argue that the jets associated with Magnetically Arrested Disks (MADs) are incapable of explaining these observations; rather, hadronic interactions within the accretion disk itself are required to produce these photons. Our findings indicate a discrepancy: simulations of MADs predict gamma-ray energies and luminosities significantly lower than those actually measured, as the jet is too constricted and short-lived for external proton cooling lengths to extend beyond hadronic time scales. Conversely, protons within the disk can effectively generate the observed emissions because the disk region functions somewhat like an astronomical Poynting-flux Rocket, subject to magnetic braking and angular momentum loss via angular flux. Furthermore, we demonstrate through a numerical simulation of an GQ MR 1.1-0.34 that intradisk magnetic fields are strong enough for external proton cooling to occur before the hadronic energy dissipates, validating the feasibility of this model.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for detecting cardiac diseases early. However, the automated analysis of heart sounds is complicated by acquisitions that are highly susceptible to additive noise and distortion caused by signal degradation. This paper proposes a filtering strategy designed to enhance the quality of raw recorded heart sounds, addressing both types of damage. The suggested algorithm divides noise—estimated as stationary across short intervals—into four Gaussian sub-bands using a Gaussian Mixture Model. It rewrites each component using score and filter functions within the score-based framework for denoising. Empirical evidence from raw heart sound data confirms that these four noise levels provide sufficient reduction of both additive disturbances and convolutioanl distortion.

The swift advancement of computing technology has enabled wearable devices, such as wristbands and mobile phones, to easily gather personal health data on activities, fitness, and sleep. Deep learning models have demonstrated significant efficacy in accurately recognizing these behaviors; however, their application is hindered by the inherent difficulties of centralized data collection, including privacy concerns and security risks. In response, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework designed to facilitate the decentralized training of activity recognition models. Within this system, server-node activity models are initially fine-tuned using a small, centrally gathered dataset, then iteratively refined through a federated learning process node-to-node using分散 user data. To enhance training efficiency and accuracy, activity nodes that utilize activity data play a crucial role in the proposal. This activity level is used to fine the contribution of each model update during the federated process. In comprehensive experiments conducted on two widely used public activity datasets, our approach not only achieved state-of-the-performance by effectively recognizing five distinct human activities while significantly reducing the required training iterations compared to existing non-teacher methods. This result was achieved even though the activity information play a crucial factor in the proposal.

Secondary investigations include establishing the uniqueness and existence of solutions to a system of backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with dependent, discontinuous obstacles. This paper investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair production at the Hadron Collider Large to highlight its significance in defining robust parameter space constraints for leptoquarks and in accurately identifying these prominent new physics candidates. Unlike conventional pair production, this phenomenon is defined because two non-conjugate leptoquarks are created in proton-proton interactions via $t$-channel lepton exchange. The study outlines the essential prerequisites and catalogs the possible scalar multplets able to facilitate this mechanism. Furthermore, we conduct phenomenological analysis within various scalar extension frameworks to demonstrate the proper incorporation of this production asymmetry in reanalyzing past experimental data, thereby ensuring precise mapping of the leptoquark parameter space.

The primary outcome is the existence of a direct relationship between the (CI2-1)/(CI1-0) ratio and $T_{\rm K}$. Consequently, this ratio, when used alongside at least one reported line flux, serves as both a diagnostic for galaxy physical conditions and a non-linear probe for the (CI2-1) transition. Pulsar Timing Arrays are anticipated to detect gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries in eccentric inspiraling configurations. We evaluate the computational efficiencies of four calculation strategies for relativistic SMBHB signals: approximations, Fourier expansions, post-circular expansions, and numerical integration. We introduce a new and adaptable DNA-storage architecture that establishes hierarchical structures among files sharing the same primer pair to facilitate data updates. While previous approaches treated a 20-base PCR primer pair as a single discrete object, our model defines it instead as an autnominantly managed storage partition equipped with its unique indexing structure. We note that although mutually compatible primed are naturally limited in quantity, the internal address space within each partition is effectively expansive. By exploiting this flexibility, we realize advanced storage semantics, including logical hierarchies and robust update mechanisms. Furthermore, building on the natural characteristics of PCR prefix-matching, we devised a method for converting arbitrary indexing protocols into PCR-variants. This approach reuses variable primed extensions, targeting specific index segments to precisely locate particular objects (such as specific files or folders) within the partition. Empirical wet-lab testing underscores this proposal's feasibility, highlighting a 140-fold decrease in sequencing expenses when retrieving smaller components from a stored partition.

Accurately and quickly predicting river flow velocities is critical for various applications, such as managing flood risks, yet traditional numerical methods are often too slow for providing immediate flow velocity data during emergencies. This limitation prevents the real-time dissemination of safety information to the public. To address this, this paper introduces a deep learning-based rapid solver for shallow water equations (SWE), trained to deliver immediate predictions of flow velocities given a specific initial velocity distribution and a domain boundary. Results demonstrate that this new solver offers a substantial acceleration in providing these critical estimates compared to conventional numerical techniques.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels, allowing devices like smartphones with limited internal dynamic ranges to capture full brightness and contrast. This study proposes a technique to automatically determine exposure parameters using a camera characteristic function. Additionally, it defines a novel merging approach relying on weighted averaging through an optimization framework. These strategies have been deployed as an HDR application for mobile use, proving their practical application. Comparative analyses against existing benchmarks confirm the method's efficiency and computational effectiveness.

Causal deep learning represents a significant and emerging sub-field of machine learning, aiming to integrate structured causal knowledge into the adaptable adaptability of deep models to build more reliable and robust systems for decision-making. However, the rapid expansion in the number of deep causal models has resulted in diverse methodologies and terminology that lack unified connections. Furthermore, key questions remain regarding which models are best suited for specific contexts, the intended advantages over the leading machine learning algorithms, and the proper integration of causal diagrams for representing learned structures. This paper offers a comprehensive causal diagram framework to organize and compare existing approaches, addressing these uncertainties by positioning various models within a unified conceptual map. The resulting synthesis clarifies the primary categories of deep causal models, distinguishes their unique characteristics, outlines their optimal application scenarios, and identifies research opportunities to advance the field.

This system is specifically capable of rigorously benchmarking lifelong learning strategies.

This study highlights the possible detection of anomalous, non-iterative radial rotation in a low-mass, sub-luminous giant known to rotate nearly as if rigidly in a strict mode. Most low-moderate mass giant's do so evolve when core contraction causes a lag in envelope rotation; however, this case defies that expectation with envelope speeds matching core constraints over roughly $10^7$ years. We suggest this discrepancy may stem from the consumption of a super-Earth-sized planet, which disrupted the core and caused sudden core deceleration that was not observed. Rapidly circulating through social media on a global scale, fake news threatens users and entire communities, especially as it emerges with alarming speed. While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where accumulating large, well-annotated datasets is impractical. Furthermore, integrating knowledge about new events currently necessitates retraining models or continuous fine-tuning—a process that is often costly, inefficient, and unfeasible in real-world applications.

To solve these issues, this paper presents MetaFEND, an end-to-end deep learning solution that unifies multi-task learning, Neural Process frameworks, and knowledge graphs to generate effective fake news detectors for novel events using existing, heterogonous datasets. This approach leverates shared representations and prior information from comparable topics to build a detector capable of accurately classifying stories emerging without sufficient training data. Extensive tests on video news across multiple domains confirm the method's capability to find emergent fake stories and outperform current state-of-the-art results. Finally, real-world scenarios involving newly emerged events demonstrate that MetaFEND successfully detects misinformation.

Quantum tunneling, a process without classical correspondence that can compete with Coulomb interactions to generate complex behavior, serves as a focal topic. Silicon doped with phosphorus allows researchers to position atoms with precision and investigate the regimes resulting from this competition. However, current systems rely on wavefunctions tied to crystal band symmetries, creating inherent sensitivity to tunneling effects. This study employs scanning tunneling microscopy to directly visualize lattice-aperiodic valley interference between connected atoms in silicon. Our atomistic analysis details how envelope anisotropy, valley interference influences, and dopant arrangement affect the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. We demonstrate that exchange can be made resilient to valley interference by strategic engineering of dopant placement along certain planar crystallographic orientations, resulting in behavior analogous to a vacuum state. In this regime, maximum exchange occurs at donor orbital overlap, with pair-to-consist variations restricted to under a factor of 10 despite precise positioning limitations. This stability persists across extended distances, covering both the high-fidelity quantum computation regime dominated by strong Coulomb interaction and the strongly coupled donor arrays essential for simulation in silicon.

This method enables the modeling of systems state evolution through probabilistic dependency hypotheses and the identification of active link dynamics within such networks. We evaluate this approach on a regulated animal diet consisting of four distinct food types and the Human Macroscale Interaction (HMI) dataset, which tracks large-scale interactions between people and objects in domestic environments. Results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively identifies systemic dynamics and network topology accurately. Furthermore, the model parameters yield biological insights into real-world processes and reliable robustness even when analyzing subsets of data or incomplete information containing missing links. Through this work, we establish an advanced protocol for leveraging AI to understand complex systems by mapping their structural and dynamic characteristics.

Feature extraction offers a viable strategy to mitigate dimensionality challenges within high-dimensional datasets. As a prevalent self-supervised learning technique, contrastive learning has recently attracted substantial interest. In this research, we introduced a unified framework grounded in a novel interpretation of contrastive learning, applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework first establishes two contrastive (CL) graphs to distinctly identify positive and negative pairs; subsequently, the projection matrix is obtained by minimizing the corresponding contrastive loss function to integrate information from both similar and dissimilar examples for unifying unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, we detail three methodologies: one unsupervised CL approach, along with two supervised CL variants. Extensive numerical tests across five real-world datasets highlight the framework's superior performance relative to state-of-the-art methods.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit human-like capabilities, they often lack up-to-date and factually precise knowledge, a shortcoming rooted in their statistical nature and reliance on training data. To address this limitation, we introduce a self-play technique designed to inject structured knowledge into an base LLA, referred to as Skill. Our approach begins by converting a specific real-world knowledge base into an appropriate self-play environment for an initial version of a base LLA, creating a game-like interaction where agents compete. This competitive and cooperative dynamic, including both team-based and generational self-play variants, enables the initial version to acquire the knowledge embedded in the external database, transforming it into a capability intrinsic to the model. Unlike methods that depend on demonstration of the desired output format or guidance, our technique does not require initial version of a model known to solve the task successfully. When the initial version is compared to other approaches on three different tasks that involve looking up information, answering questions, and summing, the skills model outperforms the baselines, demonstrating that our method effectively enables initial performance improvements guided by incorporated knowledge.

We examine three independent Jaynes-Cummings systems involving atom pairs where correlations exist between some atoms while the third remains initially uncorrelated. Our investigation focuses on the criteria required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. We determine that creating genuine multipartite entanglement is unattainable if the interaction cavity of an initially uncorrelated atom shares only classical correlations with any other cavity. Furthermore, we observe that if the interaction cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with any other cavity, the resulting atomic states *can* exhibit genuine multipartite entanglement. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite-entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions.

Nanometer-thick rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys, characterized by their precisely engineered compositions and robust out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, are currently the subject of intense research for applications involving ultrafast magnetophotonics. However, simultaneously achieving the lateral nanosizing essential for device miniaturization and retaining tunable optomagnetic performance along with preserved magnetic anisotropy remains a significant challenge. This integration constructs micron-scale magnetophotonic crystals that produce sharp and narrow magneto-optical resonances, which can be precisely manipulated by both external magnetic fields and the incidence direction of incident light. Ultimately, this stable magnetophotonic crystal establishes a platform for developing novel, high-symmetry optical directionality sensors and creating foundational structures for all-optical magnetization switching in ferrimagnetic RE-TM systems assisted by plasmonics.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, wherein a smaller "student" model mimics the soft probability outputs of a large "teacher" network. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the input training data and the internal parameters of the white-box teacher transfer; however, constraints such as storage limits or privacy concerns in practical deployments often make these prerequisites unattainable. This work introduces a novel black-box distillation framework that overcomes these obstacles by training the student model using only the teacher network, without needing training data or insight into the teacher's internal weights. Furthermore, we extend this black-box approach to achieve zero-shot knowledge transfer, enabling the student network to handle inputs entirely distinct from those used during original training. Valuable assessments across various tasks—including image classification, natural language tasking, speech recognition, and audio event detection—confirm that our method outperforms existing techniques both in distillation efficiency and final task performance.

Chances like attending college can boost upward mobility, allowing people to reach socioeconomic levels higher than their parents achieved. This study introduces a dynamic model to optimally allocate such opportunities in societies characterized by limited mobility fluidity, highlighting a trade-off between the immediate benefits of these investments and their capacity to elevate the status of recipients, thereby benefitning future generations. We illustrate how optimal allocation decisions emerge from continuous multi-generational optimization and demonstrate that these solutions generally prefer individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over merely slightly more accomplished individuals from higher statuses—essentially a system-discovered affirmative action based primarily on maximizing payoffs. Furthermore, we analyze whether such preferential treatment is temporary or persistent and examine model extensions incorporating more complex processes that dictate movement across varying socioeconomic tiers.

In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel luminosity scanning technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were conducted systematically throughout every fill during physics data collection using full-intensity beam pulses at the Compact Muon Solenoid's (CMS) Interaction Point (IP). This approach facilitated emittance and closed orbit assessments at the single-beam granularity. By precisely determining variations in closed orbit caused by beam-beam interactions, researchers were able to directly measure, quantitatively establish, and substantiate long-range PACMAN effect phenomena, with results closely aligning those generated by enhanced numerical simulations in the TRAIN code suite.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce a quantized, distributed gradient-based algorithm designed for benign agents. This section establishes the convergence of the proposed method to a vicinity of the global optimal solution, analytizing performance under both bandwidth constraints and adversarial interference. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations.

Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most vital techniques in cosmological research. Due to the faintness of this signal, scientists have built ever more sophisticated and sensitive instruments capable of scanning the sky across multiple frequencies with thousands of detectors sensitive to polarization. As these experiments reach higher levels of sensitivity, instrumental artifacts are often becoming the primary obstacle to fully realizing their data potential. We introduce *s4cmb* (Systematics for CMB), a Python toolkit designed to generate raw, bolometric-based time-domain data streams for current-generation CMB missions while realistically inserting instrumental systematic effects. *s4cmb* aims not only to evaluate the impact of such systematics on actual datasets and to inform the architecture of future detectors but also to create more authentic simulations essential for refining analytical methodologies.

The swift evolution in generating and distributing ultra-realistic media across social networks necessitates the immediate development of broadly applicable deepfake detection solutions. Observations indicate that existing deepfake generation techniques often introduce identifiable artifacts within the frequency spectrum of synthetic images and videos. Building on this insight, this paper proposes a new methodology known as MD-CSDNetwork, which integrates spatial and frequency domain features through cross-stitched architecture to enhance deepfake identification. Specifically, we convert image and video data to frequency domains to extract and combine multiple type of frequency domain artifacts with spatial domain features. Additionally, we directly integrate cross-stitched connections between various type of frequency domain artifacts and the spatial channels to facilitate information exchange and complementation across the network. Crucially, this integration aids in the training and inference of the model, ultimately resulting in a more robust and accurate detector for deepfakes. Extensive testing conducted on the Deepfake Challenge 2019, CAFace, and Deepfake 2.0 datasets confirm that MD-CSDNetwork significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art detection models in those three specific scenarios.

We examine a specific class of contractible, variationally efficient holographic tensor networks that function as approximate, manifestly defined quantum error-correcting codes capable of yielding power-law correlations. However, in the scenario involving a homogeneous network where the tensor also performs erasure correction, our analysis establishes a no-go result: it is impossible to simultaneously satisfy local contractibility and sustain power-law correlations. Neural network architectures for point clouds have demonstrated significant success, with widespread adoption in safety-critical domains like autonomous vehicle Lidar recognition systems. Nevertheless, recent studies indicate that these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks, which employ subtle semantic alterations like rotation or tapering to deceive predictions. This paper introduces Transformed Point Cloud (TPC), a smoothing framework designed to deliver strict and scalable robustness guarantees against semantic transformation attacks. The approach first classifies prevalent 3D modifications into additive, composable, and indirectly composable categories—for example, including shearing, rotation, and tapering, respectively—offering generalized certification strategies tailored for each group. Subsequent unique certification protocols address specific semantic transformations and their compositions. Empirical evaluations across various standard transformations reveal that TPC surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, notably increasing certified robustness against twisting along the z-axis by 63.5\%, as measured on a ±20° perturbation. The source code and model files are accessible via https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

The Jost function method has been adapted within the RPA framework to detect poles in the complex energy plane exhibiting complex RPA eigenvalues. This approach successfully identified poles associated with RPA excited states, specifically locating the electric dipole giants resonances in $^{16}$O. Despite the conventional view of the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O as a single state with significant strength and width, the results indicate that, under RPA conditions, the resonance comprises multiple poles. Each pole functions as a separate entity with distinctive widths, underlying origins, response characteristics regarding residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures.

Community detection poses significant challenges yet remains highly relevant across diverse fields, encompassing everything from power grids and atmospheric science to social and financial networks. However, addressing these issues in many dynamic systems is often difficult because the inherent complexity makes deriving traditional mathematical models for clustering impractical. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly consider their temporal behavior. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel methodology for clustering dynamical systems using only raw time-series data, thereby inherently capturing the underlying dynamics. This approach defines a distance or similarity metric between states based on the interdependencies they exert upon one another. For computational implementation, we employ the Koopman operator framework, enabling us to account for system nonlinearities when present. This allows the approach to scale effectively to large datasets. We validate the method's viability on two distinct domains: first, we analyze atmospheric variability by partitioning the four-dimensional atmospheric state space into regions with localized dynamics, supported by strong empirical evidence; second, we present a case study on New York City's subway metro system to demonstrate how the technique can be applied to real-world transportation networks; together, these scenarios illustrate both the practical applicability and the potential of the proposed framework.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly with either inaccurate gradient estimates or poor-quality sentence embeddings. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN to feed sparse, semantically meaningful sentence representations to the discriminator. This is achieved by treating the embedding matrix as an over-complete dictionary, approximating generator output features at each timestep through a linear combination of only a few selected word embeddings. These robust semantic representations streamline adversarial learning and ensure full differentiability, while empirical results across multiple datasets demonstrate performance gains, particularly improving BLEU scores for whole sequences.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. Our results indicate that the statistical pair distribution of inhabited planetary systems can effectively detect interstellar transfer of life under the specific condition that ejecta move with sufficient divergence relative to stellar motions. By offering heuristic estimates of key parameters in different astrophysical contexts, we conclude that open and globular clusters are the most suitable regions for testing this hypothesis.

A core focus of animal populations research is understanding how space is used and how resources are selected, a topic often addressed through telemetry data and resource selection functions (RSF). Wildlife research also heavily emphasizes estimating and modeling population density and size; recent advancements in spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models facilitate the analysis of individually tagged animals alongside those captured without specific covariate data. Concurrently, models have been developed to assess the likelihood of these untagged individuals utilizing specific habitat features—effectively serving as the analogue to RSF for captured-but-untagged entities in SCR frameworks.

In this study, we integrate SCR with RSF by formulating a likelihood that combines: (i) the sub-sampling of marked individuals within the capture process, (ii) the encounter probabilities associated with SCR, and (iii) the relationship between the probability of an individual being present at a specific location and the predicted resource availability. We demonstrate the application of this unified model through a field experiment involving badgers, where we estimated their population parameters alongside the effects of various habitats on presence. Our proposed framework offers a general approach for analyzing the intersection of spatial capture-recruitment data and information regarding environmental covariates, specifically enabling researchers to estimate the relative impacts of the habitat on both the activity centers of all individuals (as inferred from RSF) as well as their population density and persistence characteristics.

A primary benefit is the capability to examine a comprehensive set of connectivity patterns efficiently; as a test case, we analyze a three-layer structure and observe that heterogeneity in coupling patterns induces variability in state stability, despite mean field intensities remaining unchanged.

We address the fundamental task of counting nodes in a network of unknown dimensions, which is sparsely connected and plagued by a significant volume of Byzantine actors. Within a full-information model—where adversaries possess complete knowledge of the entire network state at every step, including stochastic decisions made by all agents, hold unlimited computational capabilities, and can deviate arbitrarily from protocols—their capabilities remain unconstricted. A primary advancement of this work is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estim ating network size despite large groups of Byzantine nodes. specifically, it accurately assesses the size of sparse networks possessing a small-world expander property, even when compromised by up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ adversaries ($n$ being the unknown network size, and $\delta$ any small yet fixed positive constant). The proposed method yields, with high probability, a constant-factor logarithmic approximation of $\log(n)$, with the precise total size becoming known across at least a ($1 - \epsilon$) fraction for any fixed $\epsilon$. Given that the approach remains fully decentralized and easy to deploy with minimal implementation weightiness. Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states. This research proposes an integrative, nonparametric technique for short-term queue length estimation, utilizing partial queue observations on a cycle-by-cycle basis collected from probe vehicles. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on random arrival assumptions or the need for primary parameter calibration, this method employs straightforward algebraic formulations contingent solely on signal timing. Specifically, for a given approach lane, conditional queue lengths are modeled using a Negative Hypergeometric distribution based on probe location, counts, timestamp, and time intervals (such as signal phase termination). Field test data comparing these nonparametric estimators against both parametric models and standard Highway Capacity Manual methods demonstrates that the new technique achieves parity in accuracy when estimating queue lengths.

Numerical relativity simulations involving non-trivial matter configurations require solving the ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraints to determine initial metric data. This study introduces a novel method grounded in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Rather than treating mean curvature ($K$) as a fixed value and solving the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation, this new scheme involves selecting a specific conformal factor to derive $K$ via an algebraic equation. This approach circumvents the challenges posed by solution existence and uniqueness issues associated with the elliptic constraint, doing so without resorting to the typical rescaling of source terms, a feature that is especially crucial when sources are fundamental fields, where reconstructing their original configuration from scaled data can be problematic. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, our findings demonstrate rapid convergent results for several previously unstudied scenarios in numerical relativity: specifically $(i)$ periodically inhomogeneous spacetimes containing large random Gaussian perturbations of the scalar field, and $(ii)$ asymptotically flat spacetimes representing black holes surrounded by rotating scalar clouds.

The resurgence in research regarding magnetic materials that display a significant anomalous Hall effect despite negligible magnetization stems from the desire to control and understand these phenomena. Antiferromagnetic materials within the antiperovskite structure are a developing class unique for diverse properties derived from their intricate electronic bands and magnetic arrangements; nonetheless, reports quantifying the anomalous Nernst effect in this group remain scarce. This limitation is partially attributed to the difficulty in accurately extracting the anomalous Nernst coefficient through experiments. Addressing this, we present new experimental findings on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovkslite thin films. By utilizing the same sample and geometry for both Hall and Nernst measurements, we achieve a direct comparison of the effects and calculate specific coefficients for the anomalous Nernst response and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. Furthermore, by meticulously evaluating the thermal gradient across the sample and validating findings with finite element modeling, we substantiate the reliability of the primary results.

Imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy are essential for researching and identifying novel functional materials. Modern advances in automation and experimental methods allow these techniques to execute measurements rapidly and with greater precision, thereby generating extensive datasets. These technological leaps are most evident within synchrotron light sources. Consequently, machine learning (ML) approaches are increasingly utilized to analyze real-time data. nevertheless, conceptual and technical hurdles persist; these include the knowledge gap among general facility users regarding ML, and the complexities of integrating ML models. In this article, we showcase several representative ML strategies tailored for on-the-fly analysis across multiple National Synchrotron Light Source-II (NSLS-II) beamlines. We present these instances educatively to facilitate the incorporation of models into current experimental workflows, empowering practitioners to implement similar ML algorithms at NSLS-II or comparable infrastructures. The proposed framework illustrates how diverse ML algorithms and feedback loops can merge effectively into established experiments with minimal effort, leveraging the Bluesky Suite for experimental orchestration and data management.

Fiber-reinforced composite materials featuring nanofiller-containing polymer phases hold tremendous promise for enhancing structural integrity and enabling self-diagnosis in automated manufacturing and robotic systems. However, while beneficial, micro-cracks and other defects that compromise reliability also manifest as failures within these autodestruction mechanisms. Therefore, rapid and precise spatial mapping of such damage is essential to trigger retirement of self-reporting devices when required. This study introduces a genetic algorithm coupled with Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) to drastically refine the geographical definition of cracks within carbon-composite self-sensing sensors. Validation was conducted on a copper through-conduction defect simulated as a crack using an EIT system comprising sixteen inter-electrode configurations on a carbon-composite sample with conductive polymeric filler. Results indicate that this approach yields an 80% enhancement in the spatial resolution of through-conduction failure patterns compared to standard, unconstrained CIT methods.

A novel contribution is the provision of concrete formulations for descendant fields previously unidentifiable in physics literature, utilizing this representation to establish a systematic approach for locating degenerate fields in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville systems. Consequently, specific four-point correlation functions within these models are shown to be solvable by a higher-order (specifically third) hypergeometric differential equation.

While brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) effectively promote upper-body recovery in those suffering from spinal cord trauma, their role in rehabilitative walking support was initially less emphasized, though pioneering noninvasive EEG-based prototypes offered initial feasibility for similar applications. This study aimed to develop a high-bandwidth, low-invasive interface utilizing electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings implanted on the cortical surface to detect walking states and calculate step rates. Such a interface could eventually aid paralyzed or impaired individuals by generating haptic feedback that reinforces motor control. To achieve this, we identified features from raw ECoG data within specific frequency ranges and assessed their validity via a multivariate classifier. Application of this classifier to ECoG data collected during both stationary and actual walking allowed us to successfully distinguish between the two conditions and quantify step frequency. Achieved bandwidths reached over 9 bits per second for state classification and more than 1.3 Hz for step rate estimation. Consequently, these high-throughput data streams detected during real walking could prove valuable for interfaces offering sensory support related to locomotion.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which model data through graphs, have proven highly effective for classifying information and predicting links by learning representations and structural patterns. While these approaches offer diverse applicabilities, existing literature predominantly relies on static graph models. This limitation is problematic for highly dynamic systems where connectivity patterns fluctuate non-stationarily over time but largely go unnoticed; employing static architectures in such contexts often leads to inferior performance. By contrast, incorporating temporal variations in graph topology offers deeper system insights that extend beyond standard classification. A significant limitation in current dynamic methods is their failure to capture effective connectivity, focusing instead on raw correlation without accounting for system-wide interdependencies and potential confounding influences from indirect interactions. To address these issues, we developed D-DEC (Deep Dynamic Effective Connectivity), a novel algorithm designed to reconstruct accurate connectomes that reflect both the autonomous and confounding-independent relationships between time series nodes. D-DEC integrates structural equation modeling with dynamic linear models to enable a detailed analysis of directional influences. Evaluations using both real-world and benchmark datasets—ranging from neural data to human heart rate variability—demonstrate the method's superior performance. These results indicate D-DEC outperformed existing tools, such as Granger causality-based estimators and generic GNN models. Furthermore, an analysis of recovered connectomes applied to human heart rate variability data revealed strong directional independence links, offering new biological insights into autonomic nervous system regulation that static or simpler dynamic models failed to detect.

Animals move to achieve various goals, including foraging for nourishment, securing a viable environment, hunting, evading predators, or finding a mate, driven by the vast diversity of their biological designs. To navigate their surroundings, different organisms utilize tools such as legs, wings, fins, and alternative mechanisms. In this paper, "biolocomotion" refers specifically to the movement patterns of living entities within captured video footage. An alternative term for biolocomotion is "in the wild" motion. Through biolocomotion, one can gain insights into the underlying principles governing the architecture and operational methods of diverse biological systems. Furthermore, biolocomotion plays a significant role in established video analysis pipelines employed for surveillance, acting as a primary filter for eliminating static backgrounds—a process known as "denoising." This denoising facilitates subsequent analytical stages, such as recognizing and tracking objects moving in the frame, generally referred to as "objectives." By employing biolocomotion-denosed video data alongside associated algorithmic methodologies, researchers have achieved enhanced performance across these tasks. Consequently, this paper outlines and elucidates the denoising and object detection and tracking algorithms dedicated to biolocomotion. These algorithms are detailed within a computational framework designed for analyzing motion that occurs naturally in video footage.

Advancements in technology and big data processing have exposed critical computational challenges when handling large-scale matrix inversions and solving substantial linear system problems, prompting significant research into rapid matrix inversion methods via GPU-accelerated techniques to address scenarios where classical approaches become prohibitive. Known strategies such as Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR), Newton Iteration (NI), and Diagonal Scaled Krylov-NI (DSKNI) are highlighted, noting their respective strengths and limitations in terms of convergence speeds. To overcome these barriers, this study introduces Generalized DSKNI (GDSKI), the initial in this line of work featuring both improved general applicability and an increase in order for the proposed method. Mathematical proofs establish that GDSKI converges under broader conditions than the original DSKNI, while also demonstrating its efficiency as a second-order algorithm, potentially cutting solution times in half. Comparative analyses against other iterations reveal superior performance by our method across various problems, with specific comparisons indicating that although real-world applications may not always permit the optimal theoretical performance, our method still offers notable advantages. Specifically compared with SOR solutions, our approach exhibits higher efficiency than first-order approaches, specifically proving around half the speed of traditional approaches in this study. Moreover, superior general performance was exhibited by our method compared with other approaches, specifically proving around second-order performance in this study.

The findings reveal that spatial randomness and binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter ranges. Within this newly formed topological Anderson insulator, the bulk states localization, verified by mean chiral displacement in systems ranging from photonic to atomic arrangements is indicated by high inverse participation ratio in momentum and real space. Furthermore, the analytical results derived from a self-consistent Born approximation and the localization of zero energy bulk modes, show consistent phase transitions in respect of the system's mean chiral displacement. The relationship between the system's bimodal bimodity and the presence or absence of the Anderson topological insulator is discussed, with analysis focused upon how mean chiral displacement could serve a detector to examine topological states in these cases. On the basis of this work, the scope of the Anderson topological insulator has been broadened, with implications drawn for other topological phases subject to similar disruptions.

Contextual linear bandits represent a well-established and significant model with diverse practical applications, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless domains where bandwidth constraints pose performance bottlenecks, particularly within high-dimensional space contexts involving large dimensions. This paper addresses a distributed implementation of the contextual linear bandits problem in memory-limited environments, where geographically dispersed agents collect contextual data and select actions, yet the remote learning modeler executes the core algorithm without direct access to the context data. Assuming context data originates from an inherent distribution, the proposal presents a learning approach requiring approximately 5d bits of communication context-per for scenarios with an undisclosed distribution, contrasting with zero bits context-per for scenarios with full distribution awareness, both meeting nearly identical regret bounds relative to contexts with direct modeler observation. This previously referenced bound, applicable for unknown context data distribution, contrasts with another bound, applicable when context distribution is completely known, that requires directly observing context by agent. The suggested approach represents a substantive improvement over existing methodologies in terms of communication efficiency, specifically regarding context exploration. For the unknown context distribution scenario, our methodology offers near-optimality, whereas the optimal design for the known context distribution remains an area of investigation. A numerical simulation supports these theoretical results and demonstrates the practical viability of the proposed framework.

We present findings from an application of Event Shape Engineering in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}=2.76$ TeV. Events were sorted within the same centrality class but with varying degrees of flow, allowing for an examination of different initial geometric configurations. The study demonstrates that event-shape selection influences the elliptic flow coefficient ($v_2$) independently of transverse momentum (${p_\rm{T}}$); this $ {p_\rm{T}}$ dependence, or the lack thereof in the effect, aligns with expectations that such variations in geometry drive initial fluctuations. Transverse momentum distributions measured across multiple centrality classes were analyzed. The vertical shear instability (VSI) involves hydrodynamical processes requiring swift gas cooling; it is posited to function in the outer sectors of protoplanetary disks. Although the VSI generates vertical turbulent motions capable of influencing dust accumulation and sinking, dust dynamics can conversely dampen the instability: reduced gas opacity due to dust removal hampers cooling in the already thin outer regions. Utilizing linear analysis, this research quantifies how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. By devising a cooling timescale model that accounts for dust maturation beyond one micron and size-dependent sedimentation, we integrate it with linear stability analysis to determine VSI activity regions (the "VSI zones"). Results indicate that dust growth and vertical migration cause significant stabilization of the VSI in outer disk areas that were previously turbulent with constant dust conditions. Specifically, at 50 astronomical units (AU), the HVI zone narrows from roughly ±1.8H (H denoting the disk midplane scale height) to approximately ±07H due to dust-driven cooling reductions. Such limited cooling zones are posited to be primary areas for the accumulation of super-Earth-forming solids. However, the VSI is suggested to be insufficient to explain the widespread gas depletion observed in protoplanetary disks.

The rise of outsourcing training and the ubiquity of modified neural networks in production have exposed deep learning models to significant security risks, with backdoor attacks emerging as a primary concern. In a typical scenario, an adversary injects a hidden trigger into a model during training; later, when this trigger appears in input, the model outputs a predetermined backdoor label regardless of standard inference. Recently, researchers demonstrated that global average pooling (GAP) can effectively embed such triggers, yet existing methods are limited because they assume the final-layer architecture remains immutable. This work relaxes the rigidity of that assumption by allowing attackers full modification rights over the network structure post-training, enabling the creation of backdoors adaptable to various class imbalance scenarios. We introduce DynamicGAP, a novel global average pooling implementation that generates adaptive, context-aware triggers based on the given input. Since these dynamic triggers integrate seamlessly into standard activation patterns, they remain virtually undetectable through current appraisal techniques. To substantively evaluate our approach, we developed the Open-Ended Backdoor Evaluation (OPEN) benchmark, which assesses how successfully injected backdoors function across differing label-assignment strategies. Experimental results indicate that DynamicGAP markedly surpasses existing GAP-based methods in both accuracy and efficacy, even when applied to inference that mimics adversarial attacks.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic models of light propagation grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework used to investigate potential general relativistic violations in observational data. A non-unitary PPN $\gamma$ induces a systematic global parallax bias, a relationship captured by a new formula that incorporates the satellite's barycentric distance relative to the Sun, the orientation of the Spin axis, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. These simulations confirm a strong dependency of the parallax shift on ecliptic latitude, attributed to an asymmetry in Gaia's scanning protocol. This conclusion is robustly supported by further simulations utilizing a reversed precession direction of the Spin axis around the solar vector. The current work provides a major advancement over prior investigations by offering a comprehensive mathematical description, a novel formula for that systematic shift, and a clear identification of the primary sources contributing to the parallax measurement uncertainty.

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and misleading information due to the boundless volume of such data. Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. Given a parametric family $f(y|\theta)$ for $\theta \in \Omega$, let $\eta(\theta)$ represent a specific function and $G$ be an unknown mixing distribution. Knowledge Tracing (KT) applies students' historical interaction records to model their evolving knowledge states and predict their future learning outcomes. While deep learning-based approaches for KT have recently achieved significant advancements, the exact drivers behind these DL-KT models remain elusive, and their proper evaluation and analysis continue to be difficult tasks. Specifically, existing methods typically rely on proprietary and custom data cleaning workflows, impeding experimental standardization. Moreover, these studies often utilize varying protocols that fail to reflect genuine educational environments. To resolve these issues, we present *\textsc{pyKT}*, a robust Python-driven benchmark framework designed to ensure reliable cross-model assessments of DL-KT methods. This library features integrated, standardized data processing pipelines across seven datasets from diverse fields, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DL-KT models for transparent analysis. Insights drawn from our meticulous and rigorous experiments reveal key observations on optimizing DL-KT, including the finding that improper evaluation settings induce label leakage which artificially inflates performance, and that many current DL-KT improvements show negligible progress compared to the seminal DL-KT model introduced by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have made *\textsc{pyKT}* along with our comprehensive empirical results publicly available at https://pykt.org/ and invite contributions from researchers and practitioners alike.

The regulation of protoplanetary disk evolution relies on analyzing how accretion rates scale with star and disk attributes; however, utilizing the distribution of these relations as a constraint on evolutionary models requires accurately accounting for accretion fluctuations. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning effective multi-agent strategies from collected historical data, playing a crucial role in preparing systems for real-world deployment. A prevalent practical challenge is that individual behavior policies generating joint agent trajectories often exhibit varying performance levels—for instance, mixing a completely random policy with more competent medium-valued policies. In the context of cooperative games with global reward structures, standard offline MARL approaches frequently allow agents trained on random data patterns to undermine overall team performance. This study explores offline MARL with a specific focus on addressing agent-level trajectory diversity by introducing the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework. Central to our approach, the credit assigned to specific agents is determined via a differentiable key-value memory interface using an attention-based reward decomposition network, calculated entirely offline. Subsequently, this individualized credit information guides the transformation of the offline dataset into a prioritized experience replay of isolated trajectories. Through a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic enabling agents to share high-performance trajectories and train conservative online with updated policies, we tested our method in both discrete and continuous settings (including multi-agent Mujoco). Results confirm the superiority of our approach in heterogeneous and complex offline multi-agent scenarios, particularly when there are significant discrepancies in the quality of different trajectories.

Meanwhile, Federated Learning has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate privacy and security concerns within IoVs, complementing the robust, secure, distributed, and verifiable data sharing capabilities offered by Blockchain technology. This paper presents a comprehensive survey examining Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks specifically for IoVs. Additionally, the authors explore potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research avenues associated with these BC-enabled FL frameworks. Ultimately, this survey provides a foundational framework for developing contemporary BC-enabled FL solutions designed to address various IoVs data privacy complexities and real-world scenarios.

A rapidly evolving electricity landscape necessitates updated and new ancillary services to ensure the secure and reliable functioning of power grids; however, existing assessments and policy recommendations frequently fail to address the complex interplay between markets and services. In addition, ASAM features extensive policy indicators for evaluation, such as an innovative price mark-up metric and a fresh redispatch effectiveness index to validate design queries within a controlled simulation. Results for a redispatch scenario employing a multi-period all-or-none order structure highlighted three key implications: first, such order designs present minimal risk for market participants given their full activation; second, substantial orders can generate dispatch rampages surrounding delivery times, resulting in significant balance costs; and third, all recruited rampage capacities do not necessarily require utilization within a multi-period all-or-none order design which activates everything regardless of need. We apply co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to simulate player learning and test convergence within a variety of Cournot models. Our study contrasts introduced versions using "social learning" against those using "individual learning." We observe that the "social" variants successfully establish Nash Equilibrium (NE) outcomes, whereas "individual" learning versions fail to achieve convergence, even though they behave ergodically within the Markovy chain defined by "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms."

To corroborate the "social" case where NE states remain common at steady-state, while verifying the total absence of NE under the "individual learning" parameter regimes of our simulations, we adopt a dual analysis strategy applicable both directly to the simulated genetic algorithms and broadly to relevant statistical dynamics. We demonstrate that in the "social" case, NE is an attractive limit for mean field dynamics of our simulations, while the "individual" case shows these mean field dynamics have an invariant distribution supporting non-NE states at steady-state. These findings are illustrated via direct numerical analysis of the specific co-evolutionary genetic algorithms employed, as well as via general theorems on Markov mixing times.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are now integral to many safety-critical computer vision tasks, such as automated driving and human-robot collaboration. As a proof of practical application, our model demonstrates improved vehicle recognition in an end-to-end traffic classification scenario using the MIOVision dataset with ResNet-50. ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for the visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial datasets. Designed to handle "object-feature" formatted tables—controlling both numerical attributes and textual row/column labels—it integrates a suite of statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Elastic Maps (offering a non-linear approach to PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and multilinear regression, alongside K-Means clustering and decision-tree construction variants. Featuring an array of intuitive dialogs for configuring data point properties such as size, shape, and color, along with rapid 3D rendering capabilities, ViDa Expert functions as a powerful instrument. This enables users to generate interactive 3D scenes representing high-dimensional data tables while efficiently executing both foundational and sophisticated statistical analyses.
